# Intermediate Level: R for Data Science
Designed for learners who already have basic R programming skills (e.g., familiarity with syntax, data structures, and simple data manipulation).

## Prerequisites:
 •	Basic R programming (vectors, data frames, loops, functions).
 
 •	Familiarity with dplyr, ggplot2, and basic statistics.
 
 •	Experience importing/exporting data in R.

## Duration: 4-6 Sessions | Level: Intermediate

## Course Objectives:
By the end of this course, students will:

1.	Master advanced data wrangling and visualization techniques.

2.	Apply statistical and machine learning models to real-world datasets.

3.	Write efficient, reproducible R code using best practices.

4.	Work with APIs, web scraping, and relational databases in R.

5.	Build interactive dashboards and reports for data storytelling.

## Session 1: Advanced Data Wrangling with tidyverse

## Load required libraries
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
```


## Data importation
```{r}
gss <- read.csv("gsssubset.csv")
head(gss)
```


# Filter function
### filter() - subset rows
### Single Filtering Function
```{r}
filtered_data <- gss%>%
  filter(marital=="MARRIED")
head(filtered_data, 10)
```

### Double Filtering Function
```{r}
filtered_data1 <- gss%>%
  filter(marital=="MARRIED"|
           marital=="DIVORCED")
head(filtered_data1, 10)
```


# Double filter for education level
```{r}
filtered_data2 <- gss%>%
  filter(degree=="BACHELOR"|
           degree == "GRADUATE")
head(filtered_data2, 10)
```



### Multiple Filtering Function for Different Variables [Match Operator Function]
```{r}
gss_degree <- gss %>%
  filter(
    degree %in% c("BACHELOR", "GRADUATE", "JUNIOR COLLEGE"),
    marital %in% c("MARRIED", "DIVORCED"),
    sex %in% c("MALE") 
  )

head(gss_degree)
```


## get the table of multiple filter
```{r}
table(gss_degree$marital,gss_degree$degree)
```


# perform chi-square using the above results
```{r}
chisq.test(table(gss_degree$marital,gss_degree$degree))
```

### Select Functions (Selecting Columns of Interest)
```{r}
selected_data <- gss%>%
  select(sex, degree, income, marital, age, hrswrk)

head(selected_data)
```

## mutate() - create new variables from the existing ones
```{r}
mutated_data <- gss%>%
  mutate(Salary_Category = if_else(income >=50000, "High Income", "Low Income"))

head(mutated_data)
```

## arrange() - reorder rows
```{r}
arranged_data <- gss%>%
  arrange(income)
```


# descending order arrangement
```{r}
arranged_data <- gss%>%
  arrange(desc(income))
```


# summarise() - reduce data to summaries
```{r}
summarized_data <- gss%>%
  group_by(degree)%>%
  summarize(Mean_Income = mean(income),
            Median_Income = median(income),
            Min_Income = min(income),
            Max_Income = max(income))%>%
  arrange(Mean_Income)

summarized_data
```


## Convert Data from Wider to Long Format and Vise Versa
```{r}
# pivot_longer() - wide to long format
# pivot_wider() - long to wide format
# separate() / unite() - split or combine columns
# drop_na() / replace_na() - handle missing values
```


# sample dataset
```{r}
grades_wide <- tibble(
  student = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"),
  math_2023 = c(85, 92, NA),
  math_2024 = c(88, 90, 85),
  science_2023 = c(78, NA, 80),
  science_2024 = c(82, 85, 88)
)
head(grades_wide)
```


# pivot_longer() 
# Purpose: Gather multiple columns into two new columns: one for the original column names (names_to) and one for the values (values_to).
```{r}
grades_long <- grades_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -student,                # Keep 'student', reshape all others
    names_to = c("subject", "year"),# Split column names into two new columns
    names_sep = "_",                # Split at the underscore
    values_to = "score"             # Name the new value column
  )

grades_long
```



# pivot_wider() → Long to Wide
# Purpose: Reverse of pivot_longer(). Spreads key-value pairs back into multiple columns.
```{r}
grades_wide_back <- grades_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = c("subject", "year"), # Combine these to form new column names
    names_sep = "_",                   # Join them with underscore
    values_from = score                # Pull values from this column
  )

grades_wide_back
```


# separate() → Split One Column into Many
# Purpose: Split a single character column into multiple columns using a delimiter or position.
```{r}
# Create a combined column for demonstration
grades_long <- grades_long |>
  mutate(course_code = str_c(subject, year, sep = "-")) # e.g., "math-2023"

# Now split it back
grades_split <- grades_long |>
  separate(
    col = course_code, 
    into = c("subject", "year"), 
    sep = "-", 
    convert = TRUE # Automatically converts "2023" to numeric
  )

glimpse(grades_split)
```


# unite() → Combine Multiple Columns into One
# Purpose: Reverse of separate(). Merges columns into a single string column.
```{r}
grades_united <- grades_split |>
  unite(
    col = "course_combined",     # Name of new column
    c("subject", "year"),        # Columns to combine
    sep = "_",                   # Separator between values
    remove = TRUE                # Drop original columns
  )

head(grades_united)
```



#Advanced Joins with dplyr
## There are different types of joins depending on how you want to merge datasets.

```{r}
df1 <- tibble(
  id = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David"))

df2 <- tibble(
  id = c(2, 3, 5),
  score = c(85, 90, 78))
```


# Join Types:
# nner_join() – Intersection (only matching keys)
```{r}
inner_join(df1, df2, by = "id")
```


# Full_join() – Union (all keys from both tables)
```{r}
full_join(df1, df2, by = "id")
```


# Semi_join() – Keep only observations in df1 that have matches in df2
```{r}
semi_join(df1, df2, by = "id") # Returns Alice, Bob, Charlie, David?
```


```{r}
semi_join(df2, df1, by = "id") # Returns Alice, Bob, Charlie, David?
```


# Anti_join() – Opposite of semi_join; keep rows in df1 without match in df2
```{r}
anti_join(df1, df2, by = "id")
```


## Left Join Function
# A left join retains all rows from the first table, adding matching data from the second and filling non-matches with NA
```{r}
left_join(df1, df2, by = "id")
```


## Right Join Function
# A right join preserves all rows from the second table, appending matching data from the first and filling non-matches with NA.
```{r}
right_join(df1, df2, by = "id")
```


## Join Functions Using Real Data Sets from the Field
```{r}
inv_one <- read.csv("inv_1.csv")
head(inv_one)
inv_two <- read.csv("inv_2.csv")
head(inv_two)
```


### View the Inventory Data sets
```{r}
head(inv_one,5)
```


### Convert Character Variable to Factor and Sales Date to Date
```{r}

inv_one$Category <- as.factor(inv_one$Category)
inv_one$Region <- as.factor(inv_one$Region)
head(inv_one, 10)
```


```{r}
head(inv_two, 10)
```


### Inner Join
```{r}
inner_join(inv_one, inv_two, by = "Product_ID")
```


### Left Join
```{r}
left_join(inv_one, inv_two, by = "Product_ID")
```


### Right Join
```{r}
right_join(inv_one, inv_two, by = "Product_ID")
```

## Reshaping Data with pivot_longer() and pivot_wider()
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

# In-built dataset
data("airquality")  # Air pollution measurements in NYC, 1973
head(airquality)
```


### Pivoting: convert wide to long
```{r}
long_df <- airquality %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Ozone, Solar.R, Wind, Temp), 
               names_to = "variable", 
               values_to = "value")

long_df
```


### Pivoting: convert long to wide
```{r}
wide_df <- long_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value)

wide_df
```
